summary.text: If the relevant Fermat number is prime, its totient is exactly the required power of two, while every smaller positive integer has totient too small to be divisible by that power. If it is composite, factoring a hypothetical smaller candidate into its power-of-two and odd parts excludes the even case by totient bounds; in the odd case the candidate must be squarefree, and every prime divisor must be a Fermat prime indexed below $33$, so its totient is at most $2^{1+2+\cdots+2^{32}}=2^{2^{33}-1}$, contradicting the required value $2^{2^{33}}$.

full_proof.text:
Let \(\varphi\) denote Euler's totient function, and define
\[
a(n)=\min\{m\in\mathbb N:m>0\text{ and }2^n\mid \varphi(m)\}.
\]
(The set is nonempty, since \(\varphi(2^{n+1})=2^n\).) Put
\[
N=2^{33},\qquad F_{33}=2^{2^{33}}+1=2^N+1.
\]
We prove that
\[
a(N)=
\begin{cases}
F_{33},&F_{33}\text{ is prime},\\
2^{N+1},&F_{33}\text{ is not prime}.
\end{cases}
\]
Since \(F_{33}>1\), the second alternative is equivalently the assertion that \(F_{33}\) is composite.

We use the following standard facts about the totient function.

1. If \(r\ge 1\), then
\[
\varphi(2^r)=2^{r-1}.
\]
In particular, \(\varphi(2^{n+1})=2^n\).

2. If \(x\) and \(y\) are coprime, then \(\varphi(xy)=\varphi(x)\varphi(y)\).

3. For every positive integer \(m\), \(\varphi(m)\le m\), and if \(m>1\), then \(\varphi(m)<m\).

4. If
\[
m=\prod_{p\mid m}p^{e_p},
\]
then
\[
\varphi(m)=\prod_{p\mid m}p^{e_p-1}(p-1).
\]
Consequently, if a prime \(p\) divides \(m\), then \(p-1=\varphi(p)\) divides \(\varphi(m)\).

We first establish two lower-bound observations that will be used in the two cases.

### 1. No positive integer at most \(2^N\) works

Suppose \(0<m\le 2^N\). If \(m<2^N\), then
\[
0<\varphi(m)\le m<2^N,
\]
so \(2^N\) cannot divide \(\varphi(m)\). If \(m=2^N\), then, because \(N\ge1\),
\[
\varphi(m)=\varphi(2^N)=2^{N-1},
\]
and again \(2^N\nmid\varphi(m)\). Thus
\[
0<m\le 2^N\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 2^N\nmid\varphi(m).
\]

### 2. No even positive integer below \(2^{N+1}\) works

Let \(m\) be even and positive. Write its exact power-of-two decomposition as
\[
m=2^k d,
\]
where \(k\ge1\) and \(d\) is odd. Since \(2^k\) and \(d\) are coprime,
\[
\varphi(m)=\varphi(2^k)\varphi(d)=2^{k-1}\varphi(d).
\]
Assume that \(2^N\mid\varphi(m)\). We show that necessarily \(m\ge2^{N+1}\).

If \(d=1\), then \(\varphi(m)=2^{k-1}\). Divisibility by \(2^N\) gives \(k-1\ge N\), hence
\[
m=2^k\ge2^{N+1}.
\]

Now suppose \(d>1\). Since \(d\) is odd, in fact \(d\ge3\), and
\[
\varphi(d)<d,
\]
so \(\varphi(d)\le d-1\).

If \(k-1>N\), then \(k\ge N+2\), and therefore already
\[
m=2^k d\ge 2^k\ge2^{N+1}.
\]
It remains to consider \(k-1\le N\). From
\[
2^N\mid 2^{k-1}\varphi(d)
\]
we may cancel the factor \(2^{k-1}\), obtaining
\[
2^{N-(k-1)}\mid\varphi(d).
\]
As \(\varphi(d)>0\), this implies
\[
2^{N-(k-1)}\le\varphi(d)\le d-1,
\]
and hence
\[
d\ge 2^{N-(k-1)}+1.
\]
It follows that
\[
\begin{aligned}
m=2^k d
&\ge 2^k\bigl(2^{N-(k-1)}+1\bigr)\\
&=2^{k+N-k+1}+2^k\\
&=2^{N+1}+2^k\\
&>2^{N+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus in every case an even positive \(m\) satisfying \(2^N\mid\varphi(m)\) must be at least \(2^{N+1}\). In particular, no even positive integer smaller than \(2^{N+1}\) is eligible.

We now treat the two alternatives for \(F_{33}\).

## The prime case

Assume that \(F_{33}=2^N+1\) is prime. Then
\[
\varphi(F_{33})=F_{33}-1=2^N,
\]
so \(F_{33}\) is eligible in the definition of \(a(N)\).

On the other hand, every positive \(m<F_{33}=2^N+1\) satisfies \(m\le2^N\). By Observation 1, no such \(m\) has \(2^N\mid\varphi(m)\). Therefore \(F_{33}\) is the least eligible positive integer, and
\[
a(N)=F_{33}.
\]

## The nonprime case

Assume now that \(F_{33}\) is not prime. Since
\[
\varphi(2^{N+1})=2^N,
\]
the number \(2^{N+1}\) is eligible. It remains to show that no positive integer \(m<2^{N+1}\) is eligible.

Suppose, for contradiction, that
\[
0<m<2^{N+1}
\quad\text{and}\quad
2^N\mid\varphi(m).
\]
If \(m\) is even, Observation 2 gives an immediate contradiction. We may therefore assume that \(m\) is odd.

Because \(\varphi(m)\le m<2^{N+1}=2\cdot2^N\), and because \(\varphi(m)\) is a positive multiple of \(2^N\), the only possibility is
\[
\varphi(m)=2^N.
\]
We now analyze the prime factorization of this odd number \(m\).

### 3. The odd integer \(m\) is squarefree

Let \(p\) be a prime divisor of \(m\), and let \(e\ge1\) be its exponent in the prime factorization of \(m\). The totient product formula shows that
\[
p^{e-1}(p-1)\mid\varphi(m)=2^N.
\]
In particular,
\[
p^{e-1}\mid2^N.
\]
If \(e>1\), then \(p\mid2^N\), so the primality of \(p\) forces \(p=2\). But \(m\) is odd, so \(2\nmid m\). This is impossible. Hence \(e=1\) for every prime divisor \(p\) of \(m\). Thus \(m\) is squarefree, and the totient formula simplifies to
\[
\varphi(m)=\prod_{p\mid m}(p-1).
\]

### 4. Every prime divisor of \(m\) is a Fermat prime \(2^{2^k}+1\) with \(k<33\)

Fix a prime \(p\mid m\). Since \(p-1\mid\varphi(m)=2^N\), every prime factor of \(p-1\) is \(2\). Therefore
\[
p-1=2^j
\]
for some integer \(j\) with \(0\le j\le N\), and hence
\[
p=2^j+1.
\]
The equality \(j=N\) cannot occur: it would give
\[
p=2^N+1=F_{33},
\]
which would make \(F_{33}\) prime, contrary to the present assumption. Thus \(j<N\).

Also \(j\ne0\). Indeed, \(j=0\) would give \(p=2\), whereas \(p\mid m\) and \(m\) is odd. Hence \(j>0\).

We next prove the familiar fact that if \(j>0\) and \(2^j+1\) is prime, then \(j\) must be a power of two. Write
\[
j=2^k b,
\]
where \(b\) is odd. If \(b>1\), then in fact \(b\ge3\). For odd \(b\), the identity
\[
x^b+1=(x+1)(x^{b-1}-x^{b-2}+\cdots-x+1)
\]
shows that \(x+1\mid x^b+1\). Taking \(x=2^{2^k}\), we obtain
\[
2^{2^k}+1\mid \bigl(2^{2^k}\bigr)^b+1=2^j+1.
\]
When \(b\ge3\), this divisor is strictly between \(1\) and \(2^j+1\), contradicting the primality of \(2^j+1=p\). Therefore \(b=1\), so
\[
j=2^k
\]
for some \(k\ge0\). Consequently
\[
p=2^{2^k}+1.
\]
Finally, since
\[
2^k=j<N=2^{33},
\]
strict monotonicity of powers of two gives \(k<33\).

Thus every prime divisor \(p\) of \(m\) has the form
\[
p=2^{2^k}+1
\qquad\text{for some }k\in\{0,1,\ldots,32\}.
\]
Moreover, the index \(k\) is uniquely determined by \(p\), since powers of two are injective: if
\[
2^{2^{k_1}}+1=2^{2^{k_2}}+1,
\]
then first \(2^{k_1}=2^{k_2}\), and then \(k_1=k_2\).

### 5. There is not enough total totient contribution

Because \(m\) is squarefree,
\[
\varphi(m)=\prod_{p\mid m}(p-1).
\]
For each prime divisor \(p\), let \(k(p)<33\) be its unique index from the preceding step. Then
\[
p-1=2^{2^{k(p)}}.
\]
Distinct prime divisors give distinct indices \(k(p)\). Hence the set
\[
K=\{k(p):p\mid m\}
\]
is a subset of \(\{0,1,\ldots,32\}\), and
\[
\begin{aligned}
\varphi(m)
&=\prod_{p\mid m}2^{2^{k(p)}}\\
&=\prod_{k\in K}2^{2^k}\\
&=2^{\sum_{k\in K}2^k}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(K\subseteq\{0,1,\ldots,32\}\),
\[
\sum_{k\in K}2^k
\le \sum_{k=0}^{32}2^k
=2^{33}-1
=N-1.
\]
Therefore
\[
\varphi(m)\le2^{N-1}.
\]
But we already proved that \(\varphi(m)=2^N\). This would imply \(2^N\le2^{N-1}\), an impossibility because \(N\ge1\).

This contradiction proves that no odd positive \(m<2^{N+1}\) is eligible. Together with Observation 2, it follows that no positive integer at all below \(2^{N+1}\) has totient divisible by \(2^N\). Since \(2^{N+1}\) itself satisfies
\[
\varphi(2^{N+1})=2^N,
\]
it is the least eligible number. Hence, when \(F_{33}\) is not prime,
\[
a(N)=2^{N+1}.
\]

Combining the prime and nonprime cases, with \(N=2^{33}\), gives
\[
\boxed{
 a(2^{33})=
 \begin{cases}
  F_{33},&F_{33}=2^{2^{33}}+1\text{ is prime},\\
  2^{2^{33}+1},&F_{33}\text{ is composite}.
 \end{cases}}
\]
This is exactly the claimed conditional value.
